title: Working with weighted or heavy fabric
subtitle: Adjusting your setup and needle choice when the fabric is thick or dense.
excerpt: Heavy fabrics such as wool, linen twill, and canvas need a different approach from fine cottons. The needle must pass through more resistance, the hoop needs firmer backing, and thread lengths may need to shorten. This reading covers the key adjustments.
sourceNotes: Therese de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Project Gutenberg #20776. Canvas work and crewelwork chapters discuss fabric weight and needle selection.

glossaryTerms.definition: The base fabric on which embroidery is worked. In heavyweight embroidery techniques such as crewelwork and canvas work, the ground is usually a firm, tightly woven fabric that carries the stitches without distorting.

content.text: for embroidery require adjustments that lightweight cotton does not. The resistance is higher, the needle must be suited to the cloth, and the way you mount the fabric changes. Getting these details right prevents sore hands and broken needles.

Move to a larger needle size when the fabric is heavy. A size 5 or 6 embroidery needle has enough shaft length and a blunter point to push through a dense weave without the eye catching on every thread. Using a needle that is too fine for the cloth means the eye drags and the thread frays. Check the eye can pass through the cloth without effort.

Cut thread lengths shorter when the fabric is thick. A 30 to 35 cm length is generous for light fabric; on heavy fabric keep thread to 25 to 30 cm. The friction through each stitch is higher, so longer lengths wear out quickly and split at the needle eye.

Heavy fabric can be difficult to mount in a small wooden hoop without the grain pulling off true. A scroll frame or slate frame gives even tension across the full width, and is the better choice for canvas work. If you must use a hoop, add a layer of cotton tissue between the inner ring and the fabric to improve grip, and tighten the outer ring firmly.

Use a heavier thread on heavy fabric. On fine cotton, two strands of stranded cotton sit well. On wool or canvas, four to six strands or a single strand of tapestry wool gives the stitch the body it needs to cover the ground. A too-fine thread on a dense weave looks pinched and the ground shows through.
